transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
There are new details in the investigation of the mid-air attack aboard a commercial
plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the probe, has deemed the incident an attempted
terrorist attack.
NPR's Kat Lonstorf reports from Tel Aviv.
Investigators in the UAE announced that the Fly Dubai co-pilot who carried out the attack
mid-flight assaulted the captain of the plane using what's called a crash axe, a lightweight
emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jam doors in the event of
a crash.
Investigators said the attacker then tried to seize control of the plane's flight mechanisms.
The plane had 174 people on board, many of whom are Israeli.
Israeli officials had already deemed it an attempted terrorist attack.
Emirati investigators have now agreed.
Both the pilot and co-pilot are live and being questioned, and the investigation is ongoing.
Israel has said the attacker is from Oman, although that has yet to be confirmed by Emirati,
Saudi, or Omani officials.
Kat Lonstorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
President Trump made a campaign stop in Mobile, Alabama last night, rallying supporters ahead
of next month's midterm elections.
He told the crowd prices would fall once the war in Iran ends, which he said would probably
happen after the election.
Outside the rally, Democrat George Willock blamed Trump for higher costs.
"Food prices are up.
Anything you order is more expensive, largely because the price of diesel has been driven
up."
Trump supporter Patrick Burge says he's willing to pay more if it means keeping his family
safe.
"The way I see it, at the end of the day, if I got to pay a little more and a couple
of dollars extra here and there in order for my kids to be safe in the future, make sure
Iran isn't nuclear or anything like that, then I'm okay with that."
Trump takes his midterm campaign swing into more competitive territory today with a stop
in Ohio.
Mental health counselors are warning about the risks of prediction market sites.
As NPR's Bobby Allen reports, clinicians say problem gamblers are relapsing with apps
like CalShe and PolyMarket.
Prediction market sites are surging.
CalShe's data shows the $60 billion bet on the platform last month was up 2,000 percent
from 2025.
But unlike online sports books like FanDuel and DraftKings, prediction markets do not
honor so-called self-exclusion registries.
These are lists maintained by states that automatically ban gambling addicts from using
betting sites.
Mental health experts say it is a loophole that many bettors are falling into after coming
across PolyMarket or CalShe's ubiquitous ads.
CalShe and a statement says it invests in responsible trading, including its own self-exclusion
list.
But state officials say as long as CalShe and PolyMarket stay unlicensed by states,
there are fewer consumer protections.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
This is NPR News in Washington.
New York Attorney General Letitia James has been appointed to lead a renewed criminal
investigation into an alleged sexual assault at Cornell University.
The school says it supports the appointment and has committed to an independent review
of its handling of the case.
A former student is suing the university and seven former students alleging she was drugged
and repeatedly raped at her frat house in 2024.
The Food and Drug Administration has closed its investigation into this year's cyclospora
outbreak, the largest on record in the U.S., and PR's Matt Bloom reports the agency made
the announcement in an update on its website Friday.
In the update, the FDA confirmed its inspectors found the parasite in two places in Mexico.
A drainage ditch had an iceberg lettuce farm used as an independent grower for Taylor Farms
and inside a wastewater tank at their processing facility.
It remains unclear exactly how the contamination took place, but the agency says the evidence
supports a strong link between the lettuce and nearly 13,000 cases of cyclosporiasis
across the U.S. this year.
Taylor Farms blamed the contamination on an independent grower it says is no longer a
part of its supply chain.
The FDA says it will now continue some response activities to help prevent future outbreaks.
Matt Bloom, NPR News.
CBS and former NFL quarterback Tony Romo have parted ways.
His departure comes after his July arrest in Wisconsin on suspicion of driving while
intoxicated.
This is NPR News.
This message comes from Jerry.

Why?
